title: Electrical energy in modern life and engineering
intro: Electrical energy has become an essential part of modern life and is used throughout domestic, commercial and industrial activity. This section introduces its importance and the basic stages of an electrical power system.
learn: Electrical energy is convenient, easily controllable and flexible, inexpensive, clean at the point of use, and easily transmittable.
An electrical power system consists of generation, transmission, distribution and utilization.
Electrical machines perform electromechanical energy conversion: a generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy, while a motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy.

sections.heading: 1.1 Introduction
paragraphs: Electricity is one of the most important blessings that science has given to mankind. It has become a part of modern life so much that one cannot think of a world without it. Electrical energy is the primary source of readily usable energy in the world and it drives almost all present-day activities. It has played a vital role in building the present-day civilization. Modern society is so dependent upon the use of electrical energy that it has become a part and parcel of our life.
The following reasons make electrical energy superior to many other forms of energy.
bullets: Convenient: Electrical energy is a very convenient form of energy. It can be easily converted into other forms of energy such as light, heat and mechanical rotation.
Easily controllable and more flexible: Electrically operated machines provide simple control and ease of operation. For instance, an electric motor can be started or stopped by the flick of a switch.
Inexpensive: Electrical energy is much cheaper than many other forms of energy. Thus, it is economical for domestic, commercial and industrial purposes.
Clean: Electrical energy is not associated with smoke, fumes or poisonous gases at the point of use and hence provides clean working conditions.
Easily transmittable: Electrical energy can be transmitted conveniently and efficiently from one place to another.

sections.heading: 1.1.1 The role of electrical energy in modern life
paragraphs: Electricity is an essential part of modern life and is a major contributor to the global economy. Modern society is so dependent upon electrical energy that it has become part of our life. Per-capita electrical-energy consumption is one of the main metrics used for assessing economic growth and quality of life. The greater the per-capita consumption of electrical energy in a country, the higher is the standard of living of its people.

People use electricity for lighting, heating, cooling and refrigeration and for operating appliances, computers, electronics, machinery and public transportation systems. Present-day advances in science and technology have made it possible to convert electrical energy into any desired form. This has given electrical energy a place of pride in the modern world.

Modern means of transportation and communication have been revolutionized by electricity. Electric trains and battery cars are quick and non-polluting means of travel. Electricity also provides means of amusement. Radio, television and cinema, which are popular forms of entertainment, are results of electricity. Modern equipment such as computers and robots has electricity as one of the most important pillars of its development. Electricity also plays a pivotal role in medicine and surgery, for example in X-ray and ECG equipment.

The use of electricity is increasing day by day. Residential uses of electrical energy include heating and cooling. Computers and office equipment account for a large share of commercial-sector electricity consumption. The industrial sector uses electricity to operate machine drives or motors, lights, computers and office equipment, and equipment for facility heating, cooling and ventilation.

Another major application of electrical energy in modern life is Electric Vehicles (EVs). These vehicles have brought a remarkable change in the present mobility system. EVs are gaining popularity because they are environmentally friendly at the point of use and do not produce tail-pipe pollutants. Electric vehicles can also be economical for a given driving range.

The use of renewable-energy systems is growing rapidly. Electrical energy generated from renewable sources such as solar, wind and hydel power is widely accepted because the corresponding conversion mechanisms can reduce environmental degradation. Renewable-energy systems are expected to form an important part of the future energy scenario.

sections.heading: 1.1.2 Electrical energy vs Computer Science Engineering
paragraphs: Computer Science and Engineering is a subfield associated with electronics, communication and instrumentation, which developed from electrical engineering. The engineering era began with Civil Engineering, which largely deals with static systems such as bridges and buildings. Rotational energy made Mechanical Engineering revolutionary, and the invention of the generator gave birth to Electrical Engineering.

Electrical Engineering, in association with other engineering disciplines, formed the basis for the growth and promotion of Computer Science and Engineering. It is the primary responsibility of a computer-science professional to appreciate the electrical energy that makes a computer system functional. The study of electrical engineering helps in developing the logical ability needed by computer-science engineers and can support the delivery of efficient codes and programs.

sections.heading: 1.2 Overview of electrical-energy generation, transmission and utilization
paragraphs: Energy is available in nature in different forms such as heat, wind, solar, light, chemical and mechanical energy. According to the law of conservation of energy, energy can neither be generated nor destroyed; it can be converted from one form to another. Generation of electrical power therefore means converting existing forms of energy into electrical form. This process must continue continuously to meet consumer demand at all times. The input can be any form of energy, while the output is electrical energy, as conceptualized in Figure 1.1.

An efficient, convenient and conventional way of generating electrical energy is by conversion of mechanical energy into electrical energy. The device that supplies the required mechanical energy is called a prime mover. Since steam turbines and hydraulic turbines are commonly used prime movers, the location of generating units is constrained by the availability of resources such as coal and water at an elevated point.

The generating station is generally not located where the electrical power is required. Hence the generated electrical power must be transmitted to the load centres using a conductor system called the transmission system. After receiving the power at load centres, it is distributed to various consumers and utilized. The entire system consisting of electrical power generation, transmission, distribution and finally utilization is called an electrical power system.

As Figure 1.2 shows, the power system starts with mechanical power and converts it into electrical form. The electrical power generated is transmitted to the load centre using the transmission network and is then utilized for different purposes. Other than lighting and heating loads, most loads involve motion or mechanical power at their output and therefore convert electrical power into mechanical power. These are called motive loads. Motive loads constitute about 80% of the existing loads. Thus, a power system largely ends with mechanical energy, making electromechanical energy conversion very important.

Electrical machines are responsible for electromechanical energy conversion in an electric power system. A machine that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy is called an electric generator. A machine that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy is called an electric motor.

title: Electric circuit, electric network and basic electrical quantities
intro: An electric circuit, an electric network and the basic electrical quantities used to describe them are introduced here.
learn: An electric circuit consists of a source or EMF, a load, a controlling switch and connecting wires.
An electric network is the interconnection of two or more circuit elements.
Charge, current, voltage, energy and power are introduced with their basic relations and units.

sections.heading: 1.3 Electric Circuit
paragraphs: An electric circuit is a simple arrangement that consists of a source or Electromotive Force (battery or generator), a load such as a lamp, fan, heater or motor which consumes electrical energy, a controlling switch and connecting wires. The purpose of a circuit is to transfer electrical energy to the load. The schematic of a circuit is shown in Figure 1.3.
Electric current is circulated in the circuit by the EMF or source against the resistance \(R\). The current \(I\) is always proportional to the voltage \(V\).

sections.heading: Electric Network
paragraphs: The interconnection of two or more circuit elements is called an electric network. In circuits, current should pass through all the elements, whereas in networks it need not do so. A circuit can be a network, but a network need not be a circuit.

sections.heading: Analogy between electrical, magnetic and mechanical systems
paragraphs: An electric circuit has a close analogy with a magnetic circuit. In a magnetic circuit, a Magnetomotive Force (MMF) is used to pass magnetic flux \(\phi\) through an iron core that has a finite reluctance \(S\), which opposes the flux. Similarly, in a mechanical system, the driving torque \(T\) is responsible for keeping the system at a speed \(N\) against friction.

title: Circuit elements: resistance, inductance and capacitance
intro: Resistance, inductance and capacitance are the three basic circuit parameters. Their equations and energy relations are developed alongside the corresponding explanations.
learn: Resistance opposes current and dissipates energy as heat.
Inductance is the property of a coil by which changes in current are opposed.
Capacitance is the capability of an element to store electric charge.
The equations and energy derivations appear in the body with the corresponding explanations; the Key formulas box repeats them for revision.

sections.heading: 1.3.1 Circuit Elements
paragraphs: A circuit element can be represented by any one, or by a combination, of three basic parameters: (1) resistance, (2) inductance and (3) capacitance.

sections.heading: (a) Resistance
paragraphs: Electrical resistance is the property of a material by which it opposes the flow of electrons or current through it. When electrons flow through a conducting material, they collide with other atoms and lose their energy and hence their potential. The voltage drop \(V\) in a conducting material is proportional to the flow of current \(I\) at a given temperature.
\[\text{Voltage drop }(V)\propto I\]
\[\text{or}\qquad V=I\times R\]

The constant \(R\) is called resistance. The unit of resistance is the ohm (\(\Omega\)). As the current through a resistance increases, the voltage drop also increases linearly as shown in Figure 1.5. Hence resistance is a linear element.
The resistance of a material is proportional to its length \(l\) and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area \(A\).
\[R\propto\dfrac{l}{A}\qquad\text{or}\qquad R\propto\rho\dfrac{l}{A}\]
Here \(\rho\) is the specific resistance or resistivity, whose unit is ohm-metre. The resistivity of metals increases as temperature increases and hence resistance changes with temperature.
The power absorbed by the resistance is
\[P=V\times I\qquad\text{or}\qquad P=I^2R\qquad\text{or}\qquad P=\dfrac{V^2}{R}\]
The corresponding energy consumed in the resistance appears as heat and is expressed as
\[W=\int_{0}^{t}P\,dt=PT\ \text{joules}\]

Hence resistance is a passive element which consumes energy and cannot store or deliver energy. A resistor should be properly designed to dissipate the heat produced; otherwise it melts. This is why resistors used for low-power electronic circuits are smaller than those used for high-power electrical circuits.

sections.heading: (b) Inductance
paragraphs: Inductance is the property of a circuit element that is related to magnetic flux. A current-carrying conductor produces magnetic flux in concentric form around it. The direction of the flux is given by the Right-Hand Thumb Rule, as illustrated in Figure 1.7.

When a conductor of negligible resistance is made into a coil, all the flux lines gather and produce a resultant flux whose axis is called the coil axis. When this flux \(\phi\) links with a coil having \(N\) turns, the coil gets flux linkages \(\varphi\). The flux linkages are given by
\[\varphi=N\phi\]
The unit is weber-turns.
According to Faraday’s laws of electromagnetic induction, whenever the flux linkages with the coil change with respect to time, an emf is induced in it. This emf is given by
\[e\propto\dfrac{d\varphi}{dt}\]
The next relation is
\[\varphi\propto\phi\qquad\text{and}\qquad\phi\propto i\]
and then gives
\[e\propto\dfrac{d\varphi}{dt}\qquad\text{or}\qquad e=L\dfrac{d\varphi}{dt}\]

The constant \(L\) is called inductance and its unit is the henry (H). One henry is the inductance of a coil when it produces one volt in it if the current passing through it changes at the rate of one ampere per second.

According to Lenz’s law, the induced emf opposes the cause of its generation. Here the cause is the change in current. Hence changes in current are opposed by the emf produced in the coil. This property exhibited by the coil is called its inductance.
When the current passing through the coil is steady or constant,
\[\dfrac{di}{dt}=0\]
and hence no emf is generated. Therefore, inductance is the property of a coil by which changes in current are opposed.
Like a flywheel having large inertia opposes changes in speed, an inductor opposes changes in current. Hence inductance is called electrical inertia.
The electrical energy absorbed by an inductor is given by
\[W=\int_{0}^{t}P\,dt=\int_{0}^{t}ei\,dt=\int_{0}^{t}L\dfrac{di}{dt}\,i\,dt=\int_{0}^{I}Li\,di=\dfrac{1}{2}LI^2\]

Since the coil is made with a conductor having negligible resistance and is assumed to be ideal, it does not consume any energy. It stores the electrical energy absorbed by it in the form of a magnetic field. Hence, the inductor is called an active element.
Therefore, the energy stored by an inductor is
\[W=\dfrac{1}{2}LI^2\ \text{joules}\]
The important points related to an inductor are summarized as follows.
bullets: The induced emf across an inductor is zero if \(\dfrac{di}{dt}=0\). Hence a pure inductor behaves as a short circuit to direct current (DC).
The current in an inductor cannot change instantaneously, because the induced emf would become infinite and would not allow the current to change instantaneously.
An inductor stores energy only when the current passing through it changes.
A pure inductor does not consume power or energy; it stores energy.

explainers.title: What is really happening in this coil?
paragraphs: There is no separate magnetic field that we need to imagine at the start. In this section, the current in the coil creates the magnetic field itself.

sections.heading: 1. Start with the current
paragraphs: When current flows through a wire, it creates a magnetic field around the wire. If the wire is wound into a coil, the magnetic fields produced by the turns reinforce one another, so there is a stronger resultant magnetic field through the coil.
\[\text{current}\;i\;\longrightarrow\;\text{magnetic field}\]

sections.heading: 2. Flux and flux linkage
paragraphs: Magnetic flux \(\phi\) is a way of describing how much magnetic field passes through a turn of the coil. More current produces a stronger magnetic field, so for this ideal linear case, more current means more flux.
\[i\uparrow\;\Longrightarrow\;\phi\uparrow\]
If the coil has \(N\) turns, the flux is linked with every turn. The total flux linkage is therefore \(\varphi=N\phi\).

sections.heading: 3. Faraday’s law — the one idea to remember
paragraphs: Faraday’s law says that a voltage is induced whenever the magnetic flux linkage changes. A steady magnetic field does not keep creating an induced voltage; it is the change that matters.
\[\text{changing flux linkage}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{induced emf}\]

The faster the flux linkage changes, the larger the induced emf. That is what \(e\propto d\varphi/dt\) is saying. The symbol \(d\varphi/dt\) simply means “how quickly the flux linkage is changing with time.”
bullets: No change in flux linkage → no induced emf.
Slow change in flux linkage → small induced emf.
Fast change in flux linkage → large induced emf.

sections.heading: 4. Why the coil can induce a voltage in itself
paragraphs: Now suppose the current itself changes. Because the current created the magnetic field, a changing current creates a changing magnetic field. That changes the flux through the same coil, and Faraday’s law then produces an induced emf in that same coil. This is self-induction.
\[\text{changing current}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{changing magnetic field}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{changing flux}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{induced emf}\]

sections.heading: 5. Lenz’s law — which way does that induced emf act?
paragraphs: Lenz’s law says that the induced emf acts against the change that produced it. If the current is trying to increase, the induced emf opposes that increase. If the current is trying to decrease, the induced emf acts in the direction that tries to keep the current flowing.
So an inductor does not oppose current itself. It opposes a change in current. This is why inductance is often compared with inertia.

sections.heading: 6. The inductor equation
paragraphs: For an ideal linear inductor, the magnitude of the induced voltage is written as \(e=L\,di/dt\). Here \(L\) is the inductance and \(di/dt\) means “how quickly the current is changing.”
\[e=L\dfrac{di}{dt}\]
If the current is steady, \(di/dt=0\), so the induced emf is zero. If you try to change the current very quickly, \(di/dt\) is large and the opposing induced voltage is large.

sections.heading: 7. Now unpack the energy calculus
paragraphs: The source has to do work while it builds up current in the inductor. That supplied energy is stored in the magnetic field. Start with energy as accumulated power:
\[W=\int_0^t P\,dt\]
Electrical power is \(P=ei\), so:
\[W=\int_0^t ei\,dt\]
Substitute the inductor relation \(e=L\,di/dt\):
\[W=\int_0^t L\dfrac{di}{dt}i\,dt\]
The expression \((di/dt)\,dt\) is simply a tiny change in current, \(di\). So instead of adding the energy contributions as time changes, we can add them as current changes:
\[W=\int_0^I Li\,di\]
If \(L\) is constant, take it outside the integral. Since \(\int i\,di=i^2/2\), we get:
\[W=L\left[\dfrac{i^2}{2}\right]_0^I=\dfrac{1}{2}LI^2\]
So the energy stored in the magnetic field at current \(I\) is \(W=\dfrac{1}{2}LI^2\) joules.

sections.heading: 8. What these points mean
bullets: Steady DC: once an ideal inductor’s current has become constant, \(di/dt=0\), so its induced voltage is zero. An ideal inductor then behaves like a short circuit. This is the steady-state result, not the instant just after switching.
Current cannot jump instantaneously: an instantaneous finite jump in current would make \(di/dt\) infinite, which would require an infinite voltage in the ideal model.

Energy wording: the inductor absorbs or releases energy while its current changes. Once a non-zero current is steady, the ideal inductor can still have \(W=\dfrac{1}{2}LI^2\) stored in its magnetic field even though no additional energy is being absorbed.

sections.heading: The whole story in one line
paragraphs: \[\boxed{\text{changing current}\;\to\;\text{changing magnetic field}\;\to\;\text{changing flux}\;\to\;\text{opposing induced emf}}\]

sections.heading: (c) Capacitance
paragraphs: When a conductor is formed into a coil, it exhibits inductance. Similarly, when a conductor is made into two plates and these plates are separated by a thin insulating material called a dielectric, a capacitor is formed, as shown in Figure 1.10.

When a capacitor is connected across a source or battery, it becomes charged; charges of opposite polarity are transferred to the plates. Thus, an electrostatic field is established between the plates. The charge \(Q\) accumulated on the plates is proportional to the voltage \(V\).
\[Q\propto V\]
\[\text{or}\qquad Q=CV\]

The proportionality constant \(C\) is called capacitance. Capacitance is the capability of an element to store electric charge. For a given voltage, as capacitance increases, the charge on the capacitor plates also increases. The unit of capacitance is the farad (F). A capacitance is one farad if one coulomb of charge can be stored with one volt across the capacitor.
The charging current \(i\) is given by
\[i=\dfrac{dq}{dt}=\dfrac{d(CV)}{dt}=C\dfrac{dV}{dt}\]
The energy absorbed by the capacitor is
\[W=\int_{0}^{t}P\,dt=\int_{0}^{t}Vi\,dt=\int_{0}^{t}V\,C\dfrac{dV}{dt}\,dt=\dfrac{1}{2}CV^2\]

Neglecting the resistance of the connecting wires and electrodes and assuming no leakage current through the dielectric, the energy input to the capacitor is stored in the capacitor in the form of an electrostatic field.
Energy stored in the capacitor is
\[W=\dfrac{1}{2}CV^2\ \text{joules}\]
As the capacitor stores energy and does not consume energy, it is called an active element. The important points related to a capacitor are summarized as follows.
bullets: The current in a capacitor is zero if the voltage across it is constant, \(\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0\). Hence it acts as an open circuit for direct current (DC).
The voltage across a capacitor cannot change instantaneously because an instantaneous change would require an infinite current.
A capacitor stores energy only when the voltage across it changes.
A pure capacitor does not consume energy; it stores energy.

title: Electrical energy sources: voltage, current, independent and dependent sources
intro: Electrical energy sources are classified as voltage sources and current sources, and also as independent and dependent sources.
learn: Voltage sources supply different currents at a given voltage; current sources supply different voltages at a constant current.
Sources may be independent or dependent (controlled).
Dependent sources are VCVS, CCVS, VCCS and CCCS.
Ideal voltage source → voltage stays fixed; practical voltage source → internal series resistance causes terminal voltage to fall as current increases.
Ideal current source → current stays fixed; practical current source → internal parallel resistance diverts some current, so delivered current falls as terminal voltage rises.

sections.heading: 1.3.2 Electrical Energy Sources
paragraphs: The purpose of an electrical energy source is to supply electrical energy or power to a load. These sources are broadly classified into voltage sources and current sources. Voltage sources supply different values of current at a given voltage, whereas current sources supply different values of voltage at a constant current.
The other classification of electrical energy sources is: (1) independent sources and (2) dependent sources.

sections.heading: 1. Independent Sources
paragraphs: An independent source can be an independent voltage source or an independent current source.

sections.heading: (a) Independent Voltage Source
paragraphs: An independent voltage source is characterized by a terminal voltage which is completely independent of the current supplied by it. The magnitude of voltage does not change with any variation in the connected load network.
\[V=\text{constant}\]

sections.heading: (b) Independent Current Source
paragraphs: In an independent current source, the current supplied is completely independent of the voltage across it. The strength of current does not change with variation in the load network.
\[I=\text{constant}\]

sections.heading: 2. Dependent Sources
paragraphs: In dependent sources, the voltage of a voltage source or the current of a current source is controlled by a voltage or current that exists at some other location or point of the circuit. These sources are also called controlled sources.

The symbols of dependent voltage and current sources are shown in Figure 1.13. Since the control of a dependent source is achieved by a voltage or a current, there are four possible dependent sources: (a) Voltage-Controlled Voltage Source (VCVS), (b) Current-Controlled Voltage Source (CCVS), (c) Voltage-Controlled Current Source (VCCS) and (d) Current-Controlled Current Source (CCCS).

sections.heading: Practical Voltage Sources
paragraphs: In practice, no voltage source is ideal. As the current supplied by the source increases, its terminal voltage decreases. This is because of its internal resistance \(R_s\).
The terminal voltage \(V_L\) is given by
\[V_L=V_s-IR_s\]

When \(I\) becomes zero under no-load conditions, \(V_L\) becomes equal to \(V_s\). As load current increases, the drop \(IR_s\) increases and the terminal voltage \(V_L\) decreases, as shown in Figure 1.18. Hence a practical voltage source is represented by an ideal voltage source connected in series with an internal resistance \(R_s\).

sections.heading: Practical Current Sources
paragraphs: Ideal current sources are not found in practice. As the voltage demanded by the load increases with an increase in load resistance, the source current starts reducing. Hence a practical current source is represented by an ideal current source in parallel with an internal resistance \(R_p\).
As the load resistance increases, the current through \(R_p\) increases and the load current slightly decreases, as shown in Figure 1.19.

explainers.label: Simpler
explainers.summary: Source vs load, and ideal vs practical voltage/current sources — explained simply
explainers.title: First, know which part is giving energy and which part is using it
paragraphs: A source is the part of a circuit that supplies electrical energy. A load is the part that receives and uses that energy. In a simple battery-and-bulb circuit, the battery is the source and the bulb is the load.
The words “source” and “load” in front of voltage or current simply tell you which part of the circuit you are talking about.
bullets: Source voltage = the voltage produced by the source.
Source current = the current delivered by the source.
Load voltage = the voltage across the load.
Load current = the current flowing through the load.

sections.heading: In a simple one-loop circuit
paragraphs: The same current flows around the entire loop, so the source current and the load current are the same current. With one ideal source connected directly to one load, the source voltage also appears across the load.
\[\boxed{\text{Source gives energy}}\qquad\boxed{\text{Load receives energy}}\]

sections.heading: Ideal vs practical voltage source
paragraphs: An ideal voltage source keeps its voltage perfectly constant, no matter how much current the load asks for. So an ideal 10 V source would always give 10 V whether the load draws a tiny current or a very large current.
A practical (real) voltage source cannot do this perfectly because every real source has some internal resistance. When current is drawn, a little voltage is lost inside the source itself.
\[\boxed{V_{\text{load}}=V_{\text{source}}-\text{internal voltage drop}}\]
So, as the load draws more current, the voltage available at the load may fall slightly. A real battery marked 9 V, for example, may have a terminal voltage a little below 9 V under a heavy load.

sections.heading: Ideal vs practical current source
paragraphs: An ideal current source supplies exactly the same current regardless of the load connected to it. An ideal 2 A current source would therefore keep the current at 2 A even if the load resistance changed.

To do that perfectly, however, it might sometimes need to produce an impossibly large voltage. A practical (real) current source therefore has limits: it can keep its current approximately constant only over a certain range of loads and voltages.
\[\boxed{\text{Ideal current source: current never changes}}\]
\[\boxed{\text{Practical current source: current is approximately constant within its working limits}}\]

sections.heading: The quickest way to remember it
bullets: Voltage source: “I will try to keep my voltage fixed; the current can change depending on the load.”
Current source: “I will try to keep my current fixed; the voltage can change depending on the load.”
Ideal = a perfect mathematical model.
Practical/real = what an actual device can approximately achieve.

sections.heading: Why this matters for independent and dependent sources
paragraphs: An independent source sets its own voltage or current without being controlled by another voltage or current elsewhere in the circuit. A dependent (controlled) source still supplies energy like a source, but the value it supplies is determined by some other voltage or current in the circuit.

self_checks.question: How is a voltage source distinguished from a current source?
self_checks.answer: A voltage source supplies different values of current at a given voltage; a current source supplies different values of voltage at a constant current.

self_checks.question: What are the four controlled-source types?
self_checks.answer: VCVS, CCVS, VCCS and CCCS.

self_checks.question: What is the key difference between an ideal and practical voltage source?
self_checks.answer: An ideal voltage source keeps its terminal voltage fixed and has zero internal resistance; a practical source has internal series resistance, so its terminal voltage falls as current increases.

self_checks.question: Why is the internal resistance of an ideal current source taken as infinite?
self_checks.answer: The internal resistance is in parallel. Infinite resistance means no source current is diverted through that internal path, so all the prescribed current is delivered to the external circuit.

sections.heading: 1.5 Kirchhoff’s Laws
paragraphs: Kirchhoff’s laws, in association with Ohm’s law, become a powerful tool to solve and analyze any complex electric network. These laws are (a) Kirchhoff’s Current Law (KCL) and (b) Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL).

explainers.title: How to approach a Kirchhoff’s-law problem
paragraphs: Kirchhoff problems become much easier if you separate the thinking into a fixed order. Do not start by hunting for equations. First understand the circuit, choose reference directions, and then let KCL or KVL turn that picture into equations.

sections.heading: 1. Read the circuit before doing any maths
paragraphs: Identify the voltage sources, resistors, junctions or nodes, and the closed paths or loops. Notice whether any resistor or branch is shared by two loops. At this stage, the goal is only to understand how the circuit is connected.

sections.heading: 2. Mark the unknown currents
paragraphs: Give the unknown branch currents names such as \(I_1\), \(I_2\) and \(I_3\), and draw an arrow for each one. The direction is a reference choice; you do not have to guess the real direction correctly.

If you assume a current in one direction and later obtain a negative value, the mathematics is telling you that the real current flows in the opposite direction. For example, if the assumed arrow is to the right and the answer is \(I=-2\,\text{A}\), the actual current is \(2\,\text{A}\) to the left.

sections.heading: 3. Use KCL at useful junctions
paragraphs: At a node, use
\[\sum I_{\text{entering}}=\sum I_{\text{leaving}}\]
A good strategy is to start at a node that contains the fewest unknown currents. That often lets you find one current immediately and then use it at the next node.

sections.heading: 4. For KVL, choose a loop and a traversal direction
paragraphs: Choose a closed loop and decide whether you will walk around it clockwise or anticlockwise. Either direction is valid. The loop-traversal direction is only the direction in which you read the circuit while writing KVL; it does not have to be the same as the current direction.

sections.heading: 5. Assign the sign of each voltage as you walk around the loop
paragraphs: For a voltage source, crossing from \(-\) to \(+\) is a voltage rise, so write \(+V\). Crossing from \(+\) to \(-\) is a voltage drop, so write \(-V\).
For a resistor, use \(V_R=IR\). Travelling through the resistor in the same direction as the assumed current is a drop, \(-IR\). Travelling against the assumed current is a rise, \(+IR\).
Then apply

sections.heading: 6. Write only as many independent equations as you need
paragraphs: If there are three unknown currents, you need three independent equations. Depending on the circuit, those might be one KCL equation and two KVL equations, or several KCL equations. Do not create extra equations unless they are useful as a check.

sections.heading: 7. Watch a resistor or branch shared by two loops
paragraphs: If two loop currents pass through the same resistor in opposite directions, the branch current is their difference. For example, if loop currents \(I_1\) and \(I_2\) oppose each other through a \(4\,\Omega\) resistor, the resistor current viewed in the \(I_1\) direction is \(I_1-I_2\), so its voltage term is \(4(I_1-I_2)\).
When the same branch is viewed in the \(I_2\) direction, the corresponding expression is \(4(I_2-I_1)\).

sections.heading: 8. Solve, then interpret the signs
paragraphs: Solve the simultaneous equations only after the circuit relationships have been written consistently. A positive result means the actual direction agrees with the assumed arrow. A negative result means the actual direction is opposite to the assumed arrow.

sections.heading: 9. Keep three different directions separate
bullets: Current direction: the reference arrow assigned to a branch current.
Loop-traversal direction: clockwise or anticlockwise direction chosen while writing KVL.
Voltage polarity: which side of an element is treated as positive and which side as negative.
paragraphs: These directions interact when signs are assigned, but they are not the same thing. For example, you may walk through a resistor from right to left even though its assumed current is left to right; in that case you are travelling against the current and encounter a voltage rise.

sections.heading: 10. Finish with a sanity check
paragraphs: Substitute the solved currents back into an unused KCL equation or one of the KVL equations. If the equality is satisfied, the result is internally consistent.

sections.heading: A short sequence to remember
paragraphs: Circuit → current arrows → KCL → choose loop → voltage signs → KVL → solve → interpret negative signs → check.

bullets: Choose the loop with the fewest unknowns first. Here the outer loop immediately gives \(V_1\).

sections.heading: What to notice in this problem
bullets: In a single series loop, one current flows through every element, so there is only one current unknown to solve.
For a voltage source, the KVL sign comes from the polarity crossed: \(-\to+\) is a rise and \(+\to-\) is a drop.
For a resistor, travelling with the current gives a drop \(-IR\); travelling against the current gives a rise \(+IR\).
\(V_{ab}\) always means \(V_a-V_b\). You can evaluate that potential difference along any convenient path between \(b\) and \(a\).
A useful final check is to calculate the same node-to-node voltage by a second path. Both paths must give the same answer.

bullets: Do not solve a circuit from its visual shape alone. First identify which points are actually the same electrical node.

explainers.title: Exercise 1.5.11 — understand the dependent source before solving the KVL equation
paragraphs: This problem introduces a dependent voltage source. The diamond marked \(2V_x\) is not an extra unknown current source or a fixed battery. Its voltage is controlled by the voltage \(V_x\) across the 5 ohm resistor. Once that relationship is understood, the circuit is only a single-loop KVL problem.

sections.heading: Step 1 — Notice that there is only one closed loop
paragraphs: There are no junctions where current can split. Starting from the 15 V source, there is only one path through the 1 ohm resistor, the dependent source, the 5 ohm resistor and the 2 ohm resistor before returning to the source.
Therefore the same current \(i\) flows through every element in the loop. We do not need KCL here because there is no branching node to analyse.

The arrow in Figure 1.38 assumes \(i\) upward through the left branch. That means the assumed current travels clockwise: left to right across the top, downward through the 5 ohm resistor, and right to left through the bottom 2 ohm resistor.

sections.heading: Step 2 — What does the diamond source labelled 2Vₓ mean?
paragraphs: A diamond symbol represents a dependent, or controlled, source. Its value depends on some voltage or current elsewhere in the circuit.
Here the source voltage is \(2V_x\). So if \(V_x\) changes, the dependent source changes automatically to twice that voltage.

Its polarity is shown as \( + \) on the left and \( - \) on the right. Therefore, when we walk clockwise from left to right through this source, we cross from \( + \) to \( - \), which is a voltage drop of \(-2V_x\).

\[15-8\left(\dfrac{V_x}{5}\right)-2V_x=0\]
The compact source solution prints \(4.16\,\text{V}\). The exact value is \(25/6\,\text{V}\); conventional rounding to two decimal places gives \(4.17\,\text{V}\).

sections.heading: Step 6 — Check the result using the loop current
paragraphs: From \(V_x=5i\),
\[i=\dfrac{V_x}{5}=\dfrac{5}{6}\approx0.833\,\text{A}\]
The dependent source voltage is then
\[2V_x=\dfrac{25}{3}\approx8.333\,\text{V}\]

Now add all clockwise voltage drops: the 1 ohm resistor gives about \(0.833\,\text{V}\), the dependent source gives \(8.333\,\text{V}\), the 5 ohm resistor gives \(4.167\,\text{V}\), and the 2 ohm resistor gives \(1.667\,\text{V}\).

sections.heading: What to notice in this problem
bullets: A diamond source is dependent: its value is controlled by another circuit variable. Here its voltage is exactly \(2V_x\).
Because there is only one closed path, the same current flows through every element; no KCL equation is needed.
The polarity marked on the 5 ohm resistor makes \(V_x=5i\) for the shown current direction.
A dependent voltage source is included in KVL just like any other voltage source; the only difference is that its magnitude must be written in terms of its controlling variable.
Current direction is an assumption. If \(i\) had come out negative, the actual current would simply flow opposite to the arrow shown.
Always check the final result by adding all rises and drops around the loop.

paragraphs: Suppose current tried to leave the left loop through \(C\), cross the diagonal source, and enter the right loop at \(D\). There is no second connection from the right loop back to the left loop, so there is no return path. Continuous current needs a closed path, so the current in the diagonal \(C-D\) branch is zero.

sections.heading: 2. How are the current directions chosen?
paragraphs: The directions of unknown currents are assumed. They could have been chosen the other way round. The equations still work as long as the assumed directions and signs are used consistently.
If a calculated current comes out negative, that simply means the actual current flows opposite to the assumed arrow.

sections.heading: 3. What do + and − mean across a resistor?
paragraphs: A resistor has no permanent positive or negative end. Once a current direction is assumed, the passive sign convention marks the terminal where the assumed current enters as \( + \) and the terminal where it leaves as \( - \). Potential therefore falls in the assumed direction of current.
In the right-hand 4 ohm resistor, \(i_2\) flows from \(D\) down to \(B\), so \(D\) is \( + \) and \(B\) is \( - \). Travelling from \(B\) to \(D\) is therefore a voltage rise.
In the left-hand 4 ohm resistor, \(i_1\) flows from \(C\) up to \(A\), so \(C\) is \( + \) and \(A\) is \( - \). Travelling from \(C\) to \(A\) is therefore a voltage drop.

bullets: Across a resistor: travelling with the assumed current gives a voltage drop \(-IR\); travelling against it gives a voltage rise \(+IR\).

A resistor itself has no built-in current direction or permanent polarity.

title: Star/Delta transformations
intro: The Delta–Star and Star–Delta derivations are retained before the four worked exercises.
learn: Delta-to-star: each star arm equals the product of the two adjacent delta resistances divided by the sum of all three delta resistances.
Star-to-delta: each delta branch equals the sum of pairwise products of star arms divided by the opposite star arm.

sections.heading: 1.7 Star/Delta Transformations
paragraphs: Star-Delta transformations are useful for solving networks that cannot be easily solved by regular series-parallel circuit-reduction techniques. Figure 1.45 shows the star and delta forms.
For the star connection, the resistances measured between the terminal pairs are
For the delta connection, the resistance between \(a\) and \(b\) is
\[R_{ab}^{(eq)}=R_{ab}\parallel(R_{bc}+R_{ca})\]
\[R_{ab}^{(eq)}=\dfrac{R_{ab}(R_{bc}+R_{ca})}{R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca}}\]
\[R_{ab}^{(eq)}=\dfrac{R_{ab}R_{bc}+R_{ab}R_{ca}}{R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca}}\]
Similarly,
\[R_{bc}^{(eq)}=\dfrac{R_{bc}R_{ab}+R_{bc}R_{ca}}{R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca}}\]
\[R_{ca}^{(eq)}=\dfrac{R_{ca}R_{ab}+R_{ca}R_{bc}}{R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca}}\]

explainers.label: SIMPLER
explainers.summary: What a Star/Delta conversion actually changes — and what it must keep the same
explainers.title: Think of Star ↔ Delta as changing the inside without changing what terminals a, b and c experience
paragraphs: Star–Delta conversion means replacing one three-terminal resistor network with a different-looking three-terminal resistor network that behaves the same from the outside terminals \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\).

In a star (Y) network, three resistors meet at one common centre point. In a delta (\(\Delta\)) network, three resistors form a triangle joining \(a\!\leftrightarrow\!b\), \(b\!\leftrightarrow\!c\) and \(c\!\leftrightarrow\!a\).
The individual resistor values generally change during the conversion. What must stay the same is the electrical behaviour seen from the three external terminals.

sections.heading: What does ‘equivalent’ mean here?
paragraphs: Imagine connecting the same outside circuit to terminals \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\). After the conversion, that outside circuit should experience the same terminal behaviour as before.
For a resistor network, the derivation enforces this by making the resistance seen between the same terminal pairs equal in the two forms:
\[R_{ab}^{(star)}=R_{ab}^{(delta)},\qquad R_{bc}^{(star)}=R_{bc}^{(delta)},\qquad R_{ca}^{(star)}=R_{ca}^{(delta)}.\]
So the star and delta can look completely different inside, yet one can replace the other in the larger circuit when the converted resistor values are chosen correctly.

sections.heading: Why would we convert at all?
paragraphs: Some bridge-like resistor networks cannot be simplified directly by ordinary series and parallel rules. A Star/Delta conversion changes the internal arrangement so that useful series or parallel combinations may appear.
The aim is not to change what the circuit does. The aim is to redraw that three-terminal part in an equivalent form that is easier to reduce.

sections.heading: A useful mental picture
paragraphs: Think of the three-terminal network as a black box with only \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) visible. A star and its equivalent delta are two different resistor arrangements inside the box. If the conversion formulas are used correctly, the outside circuit cannot tell which arrangement is inside.
A useful one-line memory aid is: change the internal shape, but preserve the behaviour at the terminals.

One subtle point: when we compare the resistance between a pair such as \(a\) and \(b\), the third terminal \(c\) must be treated the same way in both networks. We are preserving the complete three-terminal network behaviour, not merely matching one resistor value.

figures.caption: Fig. 1.45 · Star and Delta networks

sections.heading: Delta → Star derivation
paragraphs: To convert a delta network into an equivalent star network, equate the resistances measured between the same terminal pairs. This gives
\[R_a+R_b=\dfrac{R_{ab}R_{bc}+R_{ab}R_{ca}}{R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca}}\tag{1}\]
\[R_b+R_c=\dfrac{R_{ab}R_{bc}+R_{bc}R_{ca}}{R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca}}\tag{2}\]
\[R_a+R_c=\dfrac{R_{ab}R_{ca}+R_{bc}R_{ca}}{R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca}}\tag{3}\]
Subtracting equation (2) from equation (1) gives
\[R_a-R_c=\dfrac{R_{ab}R_{ca}-R_{bc}R_{ca}}{R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca}}\tag{4}\]
Adding equations (3) and (4),
\[2R_a=\dfrac{2R_{ab}R_{ca}}{R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca}}\]
\[R_a=\dfrac{R_{ab}R_{ca}}{R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca}}\tag{5}\]
Similarly,
\[R_b=\dfrac{R_{ab}R_{bc}}{R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca}}\tag{6}\]
\[R_c=\dfrac{R_{bc}R_{ca}}{R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca}}\tag{7}\]

sections.heading: Star → Delta derivation
paragraphs: To obtain the reverse transformation, multiply equations (5) and (6):
\[R_aR_b=\dfrac{R_{ab}^2R_{bc}R_{ca}}{(R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca})^2}\]
Multiply equations (6) and (7):
\[R_bR_c=\dfrac{R_{ab}R_{bc}^2R_{ca}}{(R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca})^2}\]
Multiply equations (7) and (5):
\[R_cR_a=\dfrac{R_{ab}R_{bc}R_{ca}^2}{(R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca})^2}\]
Adding the three equations gives
\[R_aR_b+R_bR_c+R_cR_a=\dfrac{R_{ab}R_{bc}R_{ca}(R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca})}{(R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca})^2}\]
\[R_aR_b+R_bR_c+R_cR_a=\dfrac{R_{ab}R_{bc}R_{ca}}{R_{ab}+R_{bc}+R_{ca}}\tag{8}\]
Dividing equation (8) by equation (5),
\[R_{bc}=\dfrac{R_aR_b+R_bR_c+R_cR_a}{R_a}\]
Similarly,
\[R_{ca}=\dfrac{R_aR_b+R_bR_c+R_cR_a}{R_b}\]
\[R_{ab}=\dfrac{R_aR_b+R_bR_c+R_cR_a}{R_c}\]
If all branches in the delta network have equal resistance \(R_{\Delta}\), then each equivalent star arm is
\[R_a=R_b=R_c=R_{star}=\dfrac{R_{\Delta}}{3}\]
If all star arms have equal resistance \(R_{star}\), then each equivalent delta branch is
\[R_{ab}=R_{bc}=R_{ca}=R_{\Delta}=3R_{star}\]
Thus, when transforming from delta to star the resistance in each corresponding branch decreases; when transforming from star to delta it increases.

paragraphs: The picture on the left is a delta because the three resistors form a triangle between the external terminals A, B and C. The picture on the right is the equivalent star: three new resistors connect A, B and C to one new internal centre point.
The goal is not to keep the same resistor values. The goal is to choose new star values so that the network behaves the same when viewed from terminals A, B and C.

sections.heading: Step 1 — First name the three delta resistors from their end points
paragraphs: Do not start with the formula immediately. Read the triangle first.

The 25 ohm resistor is directly between A and B, so it is \(R_{ab}=25\,\Omega\). The 15 ohm resistor is between B and C, so \(R_{bc}=15\,\Omega\). The 10 ohm resistor is between C and A, so \(R_{ca}=10\,\Omega\).

On the star side, \(R_a\) means the star arm connected to terminal A, \(R_b\) is the arm connected to B, and \(R_c\) is the arm connected to C. The centre dot of the star is a new internal junction; it is not terminal C.

sections.heading: Step 2 — Use one simple Delta → Star rule
paragraphs: For any star arm, look at the external terminal that arm is attached to. Multiply the two delta resistors that touch that same terminal, then divide by the sum of all three delta resistors.
The denominator is therefore the same for all three star arms:
The part that changes from \(R_a\) to \(R_b\) to \(R_c\) is only the pair in the numerator.

sections.heading: Step 3 — Find Rₐ: look only at the two delta resistors touching A
paragraphs: At terminal A, the two delta branches that meet are A–B = 25 ohms and A–C = 10 ohms. Therefore those are the two numbers that go in the numerator:
A useful way to say it aloud is: “For the star arm at A, multiply the two delta sides that touch A.”

sections.heading: Step 4 — Find R_b: now look at the two delta resistors touching B
paragraphs: At terminal B, the touching delta branches are A–B = 25 ohms and B–C = 15 ohms. So
\[R_b=\dfrac{25\times15}{50}=7.5\,\Omega\]

sections.heading: Step 5 — Find R_c: use the two delta resistors touching C
paragraphs: At terminal C, the touching delta branches are C–A = 10 ohms and B–C = 15 ohms. Therefore
\[R_c=\dfrac{10\times15}{50}=3\,\Omega\]
So the equivalent star is \(R_a=5\,\Omega\), \(R_b=7.5\,\Omega\), and \(R_c=3\,\Omega\).

sections.heading: Step 6 — Check what “equivalent” means with one terminal pair
paragraphs: A good check is to compare the resistance seen between A and B while terminal C is left open in both networks.
In the star, the only path from A to B is through \(R_a\) and \(R_b\), so
In the delta, there are two A-to-B paths: the direct 25 ohm side, and the path A → C → B containing 10 + 15 = 25 ohms. Those two 25 ohm paths are in parallel:
\[R_{AB}^{(delta)}=25\parallel25=12.5\,\Omega\]
Both forms therefore present the same resistance between A and B. That is the meaning of the word equivalent here.

sections.heading: What to remember
bullets: Delta → Star: the denominator is always the sum of all three delta resistors.
For the numerator, choose the two delta resistors that touch the terminal of the star arm you are finding.
\(R_a\): use the two branches touching A; \(R_b\): use the two touching B; \(R_c\): use the two touching C.
The star centre is a new internal node. A, B and C remain the same three external terminals before and after conversion.
The resistor values change, but the behaviour seen from A, B and C stays the same.

explainers.title: Exercise 1.7.2 — choose the useful Star → Delta conversion and then reduce step by step
paragraphs: The question asks for the current supplied by the 120 V battery. The easiest route is therefore to replace the whole resistor network by one equivalent resistance across the battery and then use \(I=V/R_{eq}\).

At first the middle network is not a simple series/parallel circuit because the 5 ohm resistor joins nodes c and d. That extra connection creates a bridge, so we first look for a Star/Delta conversion that will make the network easier.

sections.heading: Step 1 — First read the nodes: which resistors actually form the star?
paragraphs: The two points marked a on the top wire are the same electrical node because there is only an uninterrupted wire between them. Likewise, the two points marked b on the bottom wire are the same node.

Now look at node d. Exactly three resistors meet there: 10 ohms goes from d to a, 20 ohms goes from d to b, and 5 ohms goes from d to c. Three resistor arms meeting at one central node is a star (Y) network.

So for this star, the arm toward a is 10 ohms, the arm toward b is 20 ohms, and the arm toward c is 5 ohms. The 12.5 ohm, 15 ohm and 30 ohm resistors are outside this star and are left untouched during the conversion.

sections.heading: Step 2 — Why convert this particular star to a delta?
paragraphs: This is the useful choice because the new delta will connect the same three outer nodes a, b and c.

After conversion, the new a–c resistor will lie between exactly the same two nodes as the existing 12.5 ohm resistor; the new c–b resistor will lie between the same two nodes as the existing 15 ohm resistor; and the new a–b resistor will lie between the same two nodes as the existing 30 ohm resistor.

That means the conversion deliberately creates three obvious parallel pairs. This is the real reason for doing Star → Delta here: not because conversion is compulsory, but because it turns the bridge into ordinary series/parallel reductions.

sections.heading: Step 3 — Convert the 5Ω–10Ω–20Ω star into a delta
paragraphs: For Star → Delta, first form the common numerator by adding the three pairwise products of the star arms:
For a delta side between two terminals, divide this common numerator by the star arm connected to the third terminal — the terminal not on that delta side.
For \(R_{ac}\), the third terminal is b, whose star arm is 20 ohms. Therefore
For \(R_{ab}\), the third terminal is c, whose star arm is 5 ohms:
For \(R_{bc}\), the third terminal is a, whose star arm is 10 ohms:
The centre node d disappears in the delta replacement. The outside terminals a, b and c remain exactly where they were.

sections.heading: Step 4 — Now spot the three parallel pairs in Figure 1.47(b)/(c)
paragraphs: Two resistors are parallel when both of their ends connect to the same two nodes. Their drawn shape or position does not matter.
Between a and c, 12.5 ohms and 17.5 ohms share the same two end nodes, so
\[12.5\parallel17.5=\dfrac{12.5\times17.5}{12.5+17.5}=7.2916\ldots\,\Omega\approx7.29\,\Omega\]
Between c and b, 15 ohms and 35 ohms are parallel:
\[15\parallel35=\dfrac{15\times35}{15+35}=10.5\,\Omega\]
Between a and b, 70 ohms and the original 30 ohms are parallel:
\[70\parallel30=\dfrac{70\times30}{70+30}=21\,\Omega\]

sections.heading: Step 5 — Why do 7.29Ω and 10.5Ω become series next?
paragraphs: After the parallel reductions, the 7.29 ohm resistor runs from a to c and the 10.5 ohm resistor runs from c to b. At node c there is now no other branch for current to split into.
So the same current that passes through 7.29 ohms must continue through 10.5 ohms. That is how we know they are in series:
This 17.79 ohm path goes from a to b. The 21 ohm branch also goes directly from a to b. Because both branches have the same two end nodes, they are parallel.

sections.heading: Step 6 — Reduce the last parallel pair and find the battery current
paragraphs: Using the book's rounded intermediate values,
\[R_{eq}=17.79\parallel21=\dfrac{17.79\times21}{17.79+21}\approx9.63\,\Omega\]
So the entire resistor network seen by the 120 V battery behaves like one 9.63 ohm resistor. Now Ohm's law can be used on the whole circuit:
\[i=\dfrac{V}{R_{eq}}=\dfrac{120}{9.63}\approx12.46\,\text{A}\]
If the unrounded intermediate values are carried through, \(R_{eq}\approx9.6316\,\Omega\) and \(i\approx12.459\,\text{A}\), which still rounds to the printed \(12.46\,\text{A}\).

sections.heading: What to remember
bullets: Do not convert a star or delta blindly. Choose a conversion that makes the remaining circuit easier to reduce.
Here the 10Ω, 20Ω and 5Ω resistors are the star because all three meet at the single centre node d.
The 12.5Ω, 15Ω and 30Ω resistors are not part of that star; they stay unchanged during the conversion.
Star → Delta rule: form the common sum of pairwise products. For a delta side, divide by the star arm connected to the opposite/third terminal.
After conversion, always return to the node test: same two end nodes means parallel; one shared node with no branching means series.
Once the whole network becomes one equivalent resistance, source current is simply \(I=V/R_{eq}\).

sections.heading: 1.8 Superposition Theorem
paragraphs: The Superposition Theorem states that in any linear, bilateral network containing two or more sources, the response in any element is equal to the algebraic sum of the responses caused by the individual sources acting alone, while the other sources are non-operative.

When considering the response of an individual source, the other ideal voltage sources are replaced by short circuits and the other ideal current sources are replaced by open circuits. This theorem is valid only for linear systems.

A linear network is a network whose parameters do not change with voltage and current; its \(V\)-\(I\) characteristic is linear. A bilateral network is one whose characteristics or behaviour are the same irrespective of the direction of current through its elements. A simple resistor is an example of a bilateral element, whereas a diode is unilateral.
Exercise 1.8.1 illustrates the theorem.

sections.heading: 1.9 Thevenin’s Theorem
paragraphs: It is common to find the current in a particular resistance, generally called the load resistance \(R_L\), while the remaining circuit stays unchanged. To avoid simplifying the whole circuit for every value of \(R_L\), Thevenin’s theorem is useful. It replaces the remaining circuit by an equivalent circuit called the Thevenin equivalent circuit.

title: Sinusoidal waveforms and basic quantities
learn: A sinusoidal alternating quantity varies periodically and reverses direction or polarity; one complete cycle corresponds to 360° or 2π radians.
The basic quantities are peak value, instantaneous value, cycle, time period T, frequency f and angular frequency ω, with f = 1/T and ω = 2πf.
A phase angle locates a sinusoid relative to a chosen reference; positive and negative angular displacement indicate lead and lag relative to that reference.

sections.heading: Why sinusoidal waveforms are preferred
bullets: Many alternating quantities can be expressed as sums of sinusoids, so sinusoidal analysis provides a useful basis for more general waveforms.
Sinusoidal signals are easy to generate and transmit.
They are convenient mathematically because differentiation and integration of a sinusoid produce another sinusoid.
In a linear circuit, a sinusoidal excitation produces a sinusoidal forced response at the same frequency. This is another reason sinusoids are especially convenient for analysis and measurement.

sections.heading: Cycle, period and frequency
paragraphs: A cycle is the complete set of positive and negative values through which an alternating quantity passes before the pattern repeats. If one cycle takes T seconds, T is the time period. Frequency f is the number of cycles completed per second and is measured in hertz.
bullets: One cycle = 360° = 2π rad.
f = 1/T and T = 1/f.
For a 50 Hz supply, one cycle lasts 1/50 s = 0.02 s = 20 ms.

sections.heading: Angular frequency and electrical angle
paragraphs: If a sinusoid completes f cycles each second and each cycle spans 2π radians, its angular frequency is ω = 2πf rad/s. After time t, the corresponding angular displacement is θ = ωt = 2πft.

sections.heading: Instantaneous value of a sinusoid
paragraphs: For a sine wave starting from zero with positive slope, the instantaneous value is written v(t) = V_m sin(ωt), where V_m is the maximum or peak value. If the waveform has an initial phase angle φ relative to the reference, the general form is v(t) = V_m sin(ωt + φ).
bullets: At ωt = 0°, v = 0.
At ωt = 90°, v = V_m.
At ωt = 270°, v = −V_m.

sections.heading: Phase, lead and lag
paragraphs: Phase specifies the angular position of a sinusoid relative to a reference waveform. If one sinusoid reaches the same point in its cycle earlier than the reference, it leads; if it reaches it later, it lags. The phase difference is the angular separation between the corresponding phasors or waveforms.
bullets: A waveform written with +φ is advanced by φ relative to the zero-phase reference.
A waveform written with −φ is delayed by φ relative to the zero-phase reference.
When comparing two waveforms, first express them in a common sine or cosine form before deciding the phase difference.

sections.heading: Steady-state sinusoidal response
paragraphs: Immediately after an excitation is applied, a circuit may contain a natural or transient part as well as the forced response. For a stable circuit, the natural part dies away; the persistent sinusoidal forced response remains.
After transient effects decay, circuit voltages and currents follow the sinusoidal forcing at the source frequency. Steady-state AC analysis works with this established periodic response.

method: Write the waveform in the standard form V_m sin(ωt + φ) or V_m cos(ωt + φ).
Read V_m directly as the peak value.
Use f = ω/(2π) and T = 1/f.
Substitute the required time t into ωt + φ to obtain the instantaneous value.
For phase comparison, convert both quantities to the same trigonometric reference before subtracting their phase angles.

book_refs.note: sinusoidal representation, phase, phasor introduction and worked phase examples

cautions: Do not compare a sine angle directly with a cosine angle without first converting them to a common sine/cosine form.
In steady-state AC analysis, transient terms are omitted and only the established sinusoidal response is considered.
